cards.front: Why does a histogram use frequency density on its vertical axis rather than frequency?
cards.back: The **area** of each bar is proportional to frequency, so classes of different widths can be compared fairly. Frequency density is $\frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}$.
cards.hint: Think about what happens to bar height when class widths differ.

cards.front: What test marks a value as an outlier using the interquartile range?
cards.back: A value is an **outlier** if it is more than $1.5\times\text{IQR}$ above $Q_3$ or below $Q_1$, so it lies far outside the middle of the data.
cards.hint: Start by finding the interquartile range.

cards.front: Which pair of summaries is better for comparing two data sets that contain outliers?
cards.back: The **median** with the **IQR**, since they are less affected by extreme values than the mean and standard deviation. Then write the comparison in context.
cards.hint: Think about which measures ignore extreme values.

cards.front: Which formula gives the variance $\sigma^2$ of a data set?
cards.back: $\sigma^2=\frac{\sum x^2}{n}-\bar{x}^2$, where $n$ is the number of values. Take the square root last to get $\sigma$, which has the same units as the data.
cards.hint: Compare the mean of the squares with the square of the mean.

cards.front: A histogram has the class 20–40 with frequency 36. What is its frequency density?
cards.back: $1.8$, since $\frac{36}{20}=1.8$. The class width is 20, not 10.
cards.hint: Divide by the class width first.

cards.front: What are the steps to estimate the median from a cumulative frequency graph?
cards.back: Find $\frac{n}{2}$ on the cumulative frequency axis, read across to the curve, then read down to the horizontal axis.
cards.hint: Where does the median sit in the ordered data?

cards.front: For 80 values with cumulative frequency 30 at boundary 20 and 62 at boundary 30, what is the estimated median?
cards.back: About $23.1$, from $20+\frac{40-30}{62-30}\times10$, since the median is the 40th value and lies in the class 20–30.
cards.hint: Find the position of the median first.

cards.front: How is the interquartile range calculated?
cards.back: **$Q_3-Q_1$**, the spread of the middle half of the ordered data.
cards.hint: Quartiles mark the quarter points of ordered data.

cards.front: For the data 2, 4, 4, 5, 9, what are the mean and standard deviation?
cards.back: Mean $4.8$ and $\sigma\approx2.32$, since $\sum x^2=142$ and the variance is $5.36$.

cards.front: What does a box plot show?
cards.back: A box from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$ with a line at the median, whiskers to the most extreme non-outlier values, and outliers marked separately with crosses.

cards.front: Why should you not remove an outlier straight away?
cards.back: An outlier is not automatically an error. Check whether it is a recording mistake before removing it from the data.

cards.front: With $Q_1=12$ and $Q_3=20$, which of the values 28 and 35 is an outlier?
cards.back: 35 is an outlier. The IQR is 8, so $1.5\times\text{IQR}=12$, the upper limit is 32, and 28 lies below it.
cards.hint: Work out the upper limit before testing each value.

cards.front: How can the quartiles show whether a data set has positive skew?
cards.back: Positive skew means $Q_3-Q_2>Q_2-Q_1$, so the longer tail is on the right and the mean lies above the median.
cards.hint: Compare the two gaps either side of the median.
